title: SAE J2954_202408: Wireless Power Transfer for Light-Duty Plug-in/Electric Vehicles and Alignment Methodology
locators: Revised 13 August 2024; SAE J2954_202408
Scope: stationary light-duty EV WPT; three charging levels up to 11 kVA; above-ground surface-mounted installations
This edition specifies unidirectional grid-to-vehicle WPT; next revision is planned to address bidirectional testing and communication
Heavy-duty WPT is a separate J2954/2 workstream; dynamic applications are to be specified in J2954/3
Use alongside SAE J2847/6 communications; for bidirectional V2G, SAE notes J3072 and J2836/3 (and applicable IEEE/UL standards) are relevant
notes: J2954_202408 is an industry interoperability/performance/safety/test standard for stationary, surface-mounted light-duty WPT with three charging levels up to 11 kVA. It does not directly cover dynamic roadway, heavy-duty or bidirectional transfer in this edition. It explicitly specifies forward grid-to-vehicle transfer. The future bidirectional requirements are planned for a future revision; dynamic scope is referred to J2954/3. For the Zhang multi-vehicle research prototype, this edition is at most a partial reference for relevant stationary light-duty forward-direction aspects; it is not a compliance basis for the 30 kW/20 kHz branch, bidirectional operation or heavy-duty service. A 6/11 kW DC-rated VA is not automatically the same as an SAE kVA rating; measure actual AC apparent power before making power-class claims.

title: IEC 61980-1:2020: Electric vehicle wireless power transfer systems — Part 1: General requirements

Electrical safety, control communications, efficiency, alignment and EMC; off-board supply equipment scope
notes: Applies to EV WPT supply equipment up to 1,000 V AC and 1,500 V DC. Vehicle-side safety/EMC and maintenance safety are outside the stated scope; motion and bidirectional requirements were under consideration in this edition.

title: IEC 61980-3:2022: Electric vehicle wireless power transfer systems — Part 3: Specific requirements for magnetic field wireless power transfer systems
locators: Scope: off-board magnetic-field WPT supply equipment for stationary electric road vehicles
Sections on characteristics, electrical safety, communications, positioning and EMC

Bidirectional dynamic power transfer remains outside Part 6's published scope and is listed as under consideration. Do not infer those other domains are covered by Part 3.

title: IEC PAS 61980-4:2025: Interoperability and safety of high-power wireless power transfer for electric vehicles
locators: Official IEC webstore: IEC PAS 61980-4:2025, published 25 November 2025, edition 1.0; stationary high-power magnetic-field WPT off-board supply equipment; covers operating conditions, power transfer, electrical safety, basic communications, positioning and EMC

Publicly indexed non-IEC text preview of clauses 6.1-6.2: compatibility class A is intended for interoperable applications; class B is not intended for interoperable applications but still has safety requirements
Publicly indexed non-IEC text preview of clause 7.2.1: class A frequency 79-90 kHz; class B frequency 79-90 kHz or 19-21 kHz
Publicly indexed non-IEC text preview of Table 1: high-power rated-input bands MF-WPT4 11.1-22 kW, MF-WPT5 22-50 kW, MF-WPT6 50-100 kW, MF-WPT7 100-150 kW, MF-WPT8 150-250 kW, MF-WPT9 250-500 kW
Preview values are secondary extraction pending clause-by-clause verification against the licensed IEC publication; official IEC summary page does not expose frequency-class or kW-table details
notes: Official IEC scope: stationary high-power magnetic-field WPT off-board equipment. A publicly indexed non-IEC full-text preview reproduces a distinction between class A (intended for interoperable applications) and class B (not intended for interoperable applications but still subject to safety requirements), with class A frequency 79-90 kHz and class B 79-90 or 19-21 kHz; it also reproduces rated-input capacity bands from MF-WPT4 through MF-WPT9. These clause details are secondary-preview evidence only and must be checked against the licensed official standard before use in a normative assessment. They create a significant research hypothesis: the 20 kHz branch in the Zhang 30 kW system may fall in the class-B frequency region, which would not establish standards-defined cross-vendor interoperability. Its 30 kW VA rating is a nominal vehicle-side assembly rating, not a verified supply-side rated input, so no MF-WPT class is assigned. Do not infer conformance from frequency overlap.

locators: Green Energy and Intelligent Transportation, volume 5 issue 2, April 2026, article 100307; DOI 10.1016/j.geits.2025.100307
Abstract: same grid-side equipment interoperates with three vehicle-side assemblies rated at 6, 11 and 30 kW
Abstract: aligned grid-to-battery efficiency 91.7%-94.3%; aligned battery-to-grid efficiency 89.5%-93.5%
Open full text listed by University of Turku repository; PDF requires extraction for meter planes, mode-to-vehicle mapping, conditions and uncertainty
Full-text Table 1: vehicle-side assembly specifications: 6 kW / 400 V nominal / 380–440 V range / 190–210 mm ground clearance / 85 kHz
Full-text Table 1: vehicle-side assembly specifications: 11 kW / 660 V nominal / 600–700 V range / 160–180 mm ground clearance / 85 kHz
Full-text Table 1: vehicle-side assembly specifications: 30 kW / 550 V nominal / 420–610 V range / 270–290 mm ground clearance / 20 kHz
Full-text Table 4: per-vehicle-class BIPT-link DC-DC efficiency bands: 30 kW 93.6%-94.5%; 11 kW 94.7%-97.1%; 6 kW 94.0%-95.7%

Full-text Table 4: per-class system-efficiency slash pairs in printed order: 30 kW 92.5%/91.6%; 11 kW 93.1%/93.5%; 6 kW 94.3%/91.6%. Table header does not label slash order; do not assign direction until reconciled with figures.
Full-text Table 4: air-gap intervals distinct from Table 1 vehicle ground clearance: 30 kW 185-205 mm; 11 kW 71-91 mm; 6 kW 101-121 mm

Full-text Section 2.4 / Fig. 10 model: enabling 30 kW GA coils induces 17 A in the closed 85 kHz resonant loop; enabling low-power GA coils induces 4 A in the closed 20 kHz resonant loop. These are modeled cross-coupled loop currents, not physical measurements.
Full-text Section 2.4 / Table 2: calculated maximum core flux density 376 mT; stated ferrite saturation thresholds 530 mT at 25 C and 410 mT at 100 C.

Full-text Sections 2.5 and 4: 48 reported test points across voltage levels, directions and spatial conditions; each prototype was evaluated at eight spatial points, both directions and three voltage levels, as phrased by the paper.
Full-text misalignment envelope: Xmax 75 mm and Ymax 100 mm for 6/11 kW; Xmax=Ymax=100 mm for 30 kW.

Full-text Table 2: branch nominal/rated current and capacitor-voltage stress ratings are class-specific; exact component labels and values are preserved in the source table pending structured component extraction.
notes: Peer-reviewed open-access experimental study. The abstract reports ranges across specified operating conditions but does not identify each efficiency endpoint's exact vehicle rating, output power, meter plane, frequency, gap or uncertainty. Do not assign a range endpoint to a vehicle power class without full-text extraction. Rights review remains pending before storing substantial article-derived content. Full-text repository page exposed Table 1 design specifications: 6 kW VA 380–440 V (400 V nominal), 190–210 mm ground clearance, 85 kHz; 11 kW VA 600–700 V (660 V nominal), 160–180 mm, 85 kHz; 30 kW VA 420–610 V (550 V nominal), 270–290 mm, 20 kHz. These are paper-stated target vehicle/VA specifications, not evidence that the published efficiency range endpoints map to each class. Full-text findings extend the abstract: Table 4 gives class-specific DC-DC ranges and system-efficiency slash pairs; the slash order is not labeled in its header and is preserved without direction mapping. Table 4 coil-to-coil air gap is distinct from Table 1 vehicle ground clearance. The paper models nontrivial current in the nominally inactive resonant loop (17 A for the induced 85 kHz loop current when the 30 kW network is enabled; 4 A in the induced 20 kHz loop current when the 6/11 kW network is enabled); these are model-derived, not measured results. It also reports 48 test points and a calculated 376 mT peak core flux against temperature-dependent saturation thresholds.

locators: Renewable and Sustainable Energy Reviews, volume 239, October 2026, article 117141; DOI 10.1016/j.rser.2026.117141

title: Design of a single inductor bidirectional DC converter for V2V energy transfer: On board charger architecture
locators: Scientific Reports 16, article 19923; DOI 10.1038/s41598-026-57506-1; published 30 June 2026
Abstract: experimental validation on a 136 W prototype; transmitter DC-DC efficiency 93.4%, receiver DC-DC efficiency 95.07%, end-to-end efficiency 75.03%
Abstract: unified three-port single-inductor architecture uses four switches and one inductor to integrate grid, battery and wireless paths
Abstract: separate 1 kW interim hardware test reports PFC current THD <4% and power factor >0.99; this is not the 136 W end-to-end WPT operating point
Abstract: paper identifies future work toward a 3 kW SiC-based closed-loop prototype and V2G extension
notes: A low-power architecture study, not a commercial EV charging benchmark. The 136 W prototype results and 1 kW interim PFC test are separate hardware scopes. Exact measurement planes, air gap, frequency, load profile, statistics and uncertainties are not available in the accessible abstract. Do not conflate the 1 kW PFC result with a 1 kW wireless transfer result. The abstract's 3 kW SiC system is future work, not an achieved prototype.

title: Bidirectional Wireless Power Transfer for Electric Vehicle Energy Systems Integrating Modelling, Intelligent Control, Communication and Cybersecurity: A Review
locators: Energy Science & Engineering, volume 14 issue 9, pp. 4026-4057; first published 27 July 2026; DOI 10.1002/ese3.70608
Integrated BWPT review of analytical/frequency-domain/FE models, predictive/triple-phase-shift/RL controls, communication protocols and cybersecurity
Section on cyber-physical threats: spoofing/replay, firmware manipulation, inductive data injection/EMI, timing/latency exploitation, credential compromise, DoS and sensor tampering

Table 5 maps cyber threats to phase synchronization, ZVS, circulating current, unintended V2G and thermal impacts; proposes mutual authentication, nonce/timestamp validation, sensor plausibility, redundancy and safe fallback
Review identifies millisecond control timelines; authentication/transport handshake overhead and jitter must be treated as part of power-control design
notes: Open-access secondary review; not an experimental WPT prototype or a numerical performance dataset. The threat/effect/mitigation taxonomy informs benchmark scenario design only. Do not claim that cited attacks were all experimentally reproduced in a single WPT implementation. Rights review remains pending before copying substantial article content.

title: SAE J2954/2_202212: Wireless Power Transfer for Heavy-Duty Electric Vehicles

title: SAE J2847/6_202009: Communication for Wireless Power Transfer Between Light-Duty Plug-in Electric Vehicles and Wireless EV Charging Stations

title: SAE J3072_202406: Interconnection Requirements for Onboard, Grid Support Inverter Systems

title: An Effective Magnetothermal Mitigation Method for High-Power Wireless Power Transfer Systems
locators: IEEE Transactions on Power Electronics, volume 41, issue 8, August 2026, pp. 12591–12596

title: ISO 5474-4:2025: Electrically propelled road vehicles — Magnetic field wireless power transfer — Part 4: Safety and interoperability requirements for electric road vehicles
locators: ISO catalogue: ISO 5474-4:2025, edition 1, published March 2025; International Standard
Scope: onboard vehicle equipment enabling magnetic-field WPT, intended for passenger cars and light commercial vehicles
Covers vehicle-device safety, transferred power and efficiency, EV-device ground clearance, interoperability and test procedures
Explicit exclusions: dynamic (vehicle in motion) WPT and reverse WPT
Explicit exclusion: operation of ISO 5474-4 EV devices with supply devices specified by IEC 61980-4
Intended supply-side pairing: IEC 61980-1, IEC 61980-2 and IEC 61980-3; dynamic vehicle-side standards are ISO 5474-6 with IEC PAS 61980-5/6
notes: Correct ISO catalogue URI: https://www.iso.org/standard/81300.html. This is a published International Standard for ON-BOARD vehicle equipment, intended for passenger cars and light commercial vehicles. It covers EV-device safety, transferred power/efficiency, ground clearance, interoperability and test procedures. The official ISO abstract explicitly excludes dynamic WPT, reverse WPT, and operation with supply devices according to IEC 61980-4. It is intended to pair with IEC 61980-1/-2/-3. It is not the vehicle-side standard for dynamic WPT (ISO 5474-6) and cannot be used as the vehicle-side compliance basis for IEC PAS 61980-4 high-power supply equipment. This distinction matters: the Zhang 30 kW / 20 kHz and bidirectional tests are outside this document's explicit interoperability scope.

title: Dynamic Wireless Power Transfer for Electric Vehicle Charging Applications: A Comparative Study of SS and LCC Compensation Topologies

title: Machine Learning-Based Foreign Object Detection in Wireless EV Charging Using Planar Magnetic Induction Tomography
locators: Section 4-6: custom STM32 acquisition, 120 MIT sensor channels and 13 engineered statistical/temporal/frequency-domain features

notes: Full-text extraction makes an important distinction between same-session offline validation and live cross-session performance. Raw-value accuracy falls to 42-62% in the 50-attempt live test despite near-perfect offline figures; feature engineering plus median+Savitzky-Golay preprocessing raises the best RF and XGBoost configurations to 49/50 (98%). Active-transfer results are promising but use a small controlled test and do not establish vehicle-scale field reliability. Do not claim zero operational false-negative risk from a finite test with zero observed errors.

(2026), DOI 10.1016/j.optlastec.2026.115445, which reports a distinct 20 m indoor optical-link energy-transfer demonstration.

title: An L-S/N IPT System with a Lightweight Receiver and Primary-Side Tuning and Constant-Current Control for Misalignment-Tolerant UAV Wireless Charging
locators: Electronics 2026, 15(18), 4245; DOI 10.3390/electronics15184245; published 17 September 2026.
Sections 2–3 and Table 2: L-S/N compensation (no secondary-side resonant network), 85 kHz operating frequency, 20 mm air gap, 65 V DC-link input and approximately 100 W target output.

Section 4.2 / Figures 22–23: physical prototype tests at aligned, intermediate and maximum horizontal misalignment; maximum measured displacement 85 mm; reported DC-to-DC efficiencies 84.3%, 82.6% and 80.8%.
Figure 23 / Section 4.2: measured output currents 5.92 A, 5.97 A and 5.96 A versus a 5.90 A reference; maximum and mean absolute current-regulation errors 1.19% and 0.85%.
Section 4.3: receiver coil mass 80.0 g, passive rectifier-filter board 33.7 g, complete receiver assembly 138.4 g.

Section 3.2: a 100 mm horizontal misalignment radius is described for the designed coupler, but the largest physical prototype position explicitly tested is 85 mm; do not promote 100 mm to a measured test boundary.

Conclusion: movement after normal power transfer does not automatically trigger online re-identification; the current implementation must interrupt transfer and repeat low-voltage pre-detection. Communication-free CC-to-CV transition is not implemented.
The prototype uses an electronic load to emulate the constant-current charging stage; the reported DC-to-DC efficiency is not a measured grid-to-battery or stored-battery-energy result.
notes: Direct UAV near-field IPT experiment with a lightweight uncompensated receiver, primary-side-only mutual-inductance identification and switched-capacitor resonance tuning. Separate position tests are one prototype campaign, not independent systems or a moving-flight WPT demonstration. Preserve the paper's 85 mm measured maximum offset separately from its 100 mm model/design statement.

title: Enhanced Multi-Sine Phase Perturbation-Based System Identification for Characterizing Misalignment-Dependent Inductances in ZVS-Controlled Wireless Power Transfer Systems
locators: IEEE Transactions on Power Electronics, Early Access, 1 October 2026; DOI 10.1109/TPEL.2026.3739481.
Abstract: experimental characterization of lateral misalignment, angular misalignment and air-gap changes and their effects on self/mutual inductances and inverter ZVS.

Abstract: enhanced multi-sine phase perturbation is applied to inverter output voltage; input impedance is observed to estimate primary self-inductance, secondary self-inductance, mutual inductance and equivalent load resistance.
Abstract: frequency-control method uses estimated system parameters to identify changes and set a new optimum operating point without a primary/secondary communications link.

Tampere University research portal lists the accepted author manuscript as open access under CC BY; exact hardware power/frequency/efficiency and numerical identification errors are not stated in the accessible abstract.
notes: Relevant system-identification/control comparator for WPT misalignment, gap and load adaptation. It is not UAV-specific in the accessible metadata. The record captures its experimentally validated identification method, not an inferred power-transfer rating or efficiency.

title: Communication-Free CC/CV Phase Shift Control for SS-Compensated WPT System under Misalignment via Reflected Impedance Decoupling
locators: IEEE Journal of Emerging and Selected Topics in Power Electronics, Early Access; DOI 10.1109/JESTPE.2026.3694075; publication date 18 May 2026.
Abstract: series–series compensated WPT system with a 50 W experimental prototype.
Abstract: mutual inductance identified before charging by detuning the receiver to modify reflected impedance; equivalent load estimated online during charging.
Abstract: unified closed-form transmitter phase-shift control for constant-current and constant-voltage regulation without receiver-side sensing, communications or auxiliary converters.
Abstract: mutual-inductance estimation error below 6.4%; equivalent-load estimation error within 3.1%; steady-state CC and CV regulation error within 1% under tested coil-misalignment conditions.
notes: System-identification and charging-regulation comparator. The abstract reports a 50 W prototype and estimator/regulation errors but does not expose measured DC-to-DC or end-to-end efficiency, exact frequency/gap/misalignment matrix, output power trace or battery-terminal energy. Do not merge with UAV L-S/N prototype results; SS compensation is a distinct topology.

title: A Fixed Air-Core Beam Wireless Power Transfer for Drones: Theory, Design, and Experimental Insights
locators: Telecom 2026, 7(4), 79; DOI 10.3390/telecom7040079; published 1 July 2026.

Sections 2–3: 24 GHz Laguerre–Gaussian m=3-dominant fixed air-core beam generated with a radial line slot antenna (RLSA) and approximately 25 W class PA feed circuit; the transmitter does not electronically steer the beam.
Section 4: relative beam-position inference from segmented receiving-signal imbalance; reference receiver has monotonic detection at 0.75 m but a non-monotonic response at 1.5 m.
Section 4.3: implementation-oriented panel-rectenna receiver has a ~25 mm peak-position offset and produces approximately 406 mW total DC load power across 19 LED load outputs.

Section 4.3: PA-output reference is approximately 25 W; authors report an apparent PA-output-to-load-side DC transfer ratio of approximately 1.6%, including all downstream loss/nonideality after the PA output ports.
Data availability: beam cross-section, modal spectrum and receiver position-detection datasets available from corresponding author on reasonable request; not publicly available.
notes: Staged experimental fixed-beam microwave WPT study. It validates air-core beam generation, receiver-relative position detection and a low-power rectenna/LED load. It does not demonstrate an integrated autonomous UAV flight, battery-terminal charging, or a high-power/long-range energy-service session. The ~25 W and ~406 mW are distinct PA-reference and receiver-load boundaries.

title: Autonomous Charging and Battery Swapping for Unmanned Aerial Vehicles: A Review
locators: Advanced Intelligent Systems, Early View e70584; DOI 10.1002/aisy.70584; first published 25 October 2026.

Section 2: literature search across Web of Science, Scopus, PubMed, Engineering Village and IEEE Xplore was performed in January 2026; this search window predates Reach Power's 22 September 2026 10-hour demonstration.

Table 4 / Section 3.2.3: far-field UAV power transfer comparators include laser and microwave systems with reported output power, optical/electrical efficiency, frequency/wavelength and range kept separate.

Section 3.2.3: the review reports an earlier Achtelik et al. laser-powered 1 kg UAV flight of 12 h 27 min, with horizontal movement confined to a 5 m x 5 m area; it does not give a matched energy-meter boundary or modern reacquisition metrics.
Section 3.3: automated battery swapping can take tens of seconds to a minute; a ground station prototype completed 195 of 200 exchanges without operator intervention.

Section 4: the review concludes there are still no UAV-specific long-term charger service-life datasets sufficient for method-to-method durability comparison, and it identifies receiver/station interoperability as a major autonomy constraint.
The review distinguishes near-field IPT/CPT from far-field MPT/LPT and compares contact charging, WPT, battery swapping and power-line charging as separate autonomous replenishment methods.
notes: Systematic review of autonomous UAV charging and battery swapping. Its evidence search ran in January 2026, so it cannot evaluate later 2026 demonstrations. The 12 h 27 min laser flight is a literature-reported constrained-area endurance result, not directly rankable with Reach Power's October 2026 10-hour commercial announcement without matched geometry, autonomy, power and battery data.
